questions.q: Transition elements show variable oxidation states because:
options: The $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ electrons have similar energies and both take part in bonding
questions.solution:
In a transition element the $(n-1)d$ and $ns$ orbitals are **very close in energy**, so electrons from **both** can be lost or involved in bonding.

The number removed can vary, giving a range of oxidation states differing by one — manganese runs from $+2$ to $+7$.

Contrast a main-group metal, where only the outermost $s$ and $p$ electrons are accessible and the oxidation states typically differ by **two**, because the inner shell is far lower in energy.

Colour in a transition metal complex comes from **d-d transitions**, which require a **partially filled** $d$ subshell.

$\text{Zn}^{2+}$ is $3d^{10}$ — **completely full**, so no $d$ electron can be promoted within the subshell and the ion is **colourless**.

The same applies to $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ ($d^{0}$) and $\text{Cu}^{+}$ ($d^{10}$). This is also why zinc is often not counted as a true transition metal: it has no partially filled $d$ subshell in any of its common states.

questions.q: The lanthanoid contraction is caused by:
options: Increasing nuclear charge with poor shielding by $4f$ electrons
questions.solution:
Across the lanthanoid series, electrons enter the **$4f$** subshell, whose orbitals are **diffuse and shield very poorly**.

The nuclear charge rises steadily while the shielding barely improves, so the **effective nuclear charge increases** and the radii shrink gradually — the **lanthanoid contraction**.

Its consequences reach far beyond the lanthanoids: the second and third transition series have **almost identical radii** (zirconium and hafnium, niobium and tantalum), which is why those pairs are so difficult to separate chemically.

questions.q: The spin-only magnetic moment of an ion with 3 unpaired electrons is approximately:
questions.solution:
$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ Bohr magnetons, where $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons.

$\mu = \sqrt{3(3+2)} = \sqrt{15} = \mathbf{3.87\ \text{BM}}$

The useful values to recognise: $n = 1$ gives $1.73$, $n = 2$ gives $2.83$, $n = 4$ gives $4.90$, $n = 5$ gives $5.92$.

Measuring the moment and working backwards is the standard way of finding how many unpaired electrons a complex has, and hence whether it is high or low spin.

questions.q: Transition metals act as good catalysts mainly because they:
options: Show variable oxidation states and can adsorb reactants on their surface
questions.solution:
Two properties matter.

**Variable oxidation states** let the metal accept and donate electrons, forming intermediates that offer a lower-energy path — iron in the Haber process, vanadium(V) oxide in the contact process.

**Surface adsorption**: partially filled $d$ orbitals bind reactant molecules to the surface, raising their local concentration and **weakening their bonds**, so they react more readily. Nickel in hydrogenation works this way.

The adsorption must be **moderate** — strong enough to weaken the bond, weak enough to release the product. That balance is why only some metals catalyse a given reaction.

questions.q: In acid medium, potassium permanganate oxidizes oxalic acid to :
questions.solution:
$2\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\mathrm{C_2O_4^{2-}} + 16\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 10\mathrm{CO_2} + 8\mathrm{H_2O}$

Each carbon goes from $+3$ to $+4$: oxalic acid is oxidised to **carbon dioxide**.

questions.q: Transition metals readily form interstitial compounds with elements such as H, C and N because:
options: Small atoms occupy the interstitial voids in the metal lattice
questions.solution:
Small atoms — hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen, boron — fit into the **interstitial voids** of the transition metal lattice without disturbing it.

The resulting compounds are typically **hard, rigid, non-stoichiometric** and retain metallic conductivity.

They are usually **harder than the pure metal**, because the trapped atoms obstruct the sliding of layers past one another. Steel is the familiar case: carbon in iron's interstices is what turns a soft metal into a structural one.

questions.q: Zinc, cadmium and mercury are not regarded as typical transition metals because:
options: Their $d$ subshells are completely filled in both the atom and their common ions
questions.solution:
The definition of a transition element requires a **partially filled $d$ subshell in the atom or in one of its common ions**.

Zinc, cadmium and mercury are $d^{10}$ in the atom and $d^{10}$ in their usual $+2$ ions, so they never satisfy it.

The consequences are exactly what you would expect from a full $d$ subshell: their compounds are **colourless and diamagnetic**, they show **no variable oxidation states** (the $\text{Hg}_2^{2+}$ ion being the notable exception), and they are poor catalysts. They also have much **lower melting points**, since $d$ electrons do not contribute to the metallic bonding.

questions.q: The most common oxidation state of Actinoids is :
questions.solution:
Like the lanthanoids, the actinoids most commonly show **+3**.

Because the 5f, 6d and 7s energies are close, they also show many others, from $+3$ up to $+7$ for neptunium and plutonium.

questions.q: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment, in Bohr magnetons, of $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ in a high-spin octahedral complex ($d^{5}$). Give the answer to two decimal places.
questions.solution:
$\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $d^{5}$, and in a **high-spin** complex all five electrons stay unpaired, so $n = 5$.

$\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{5 \times 7} = \sqrt{35} = \mathbf{5.92\ \text{BM}}$

This is the largest spin-only moment possible for a $d$-block ion. In a **low-spin** $d^{5}$ complex such as $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{3-}$ only **one** electron is unpaired, giving $1.73\ \text{BM}$ — a measurable difference that reveals the spin state.

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of manganese in $\text{KMnO}_4$?
questions.solution:
Potassium is $+1$ and oxygen $-2$ each.

$(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$

$1 + x - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+7}$

questions.q: What is the oxidation state of chromium in $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$?
questions.solution:
Potassium is $+1$ each and oxygen $-2$ each.

$2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0$

$2 + 2x - 14 = 0$

$2x = 12 \Rightarrow x = \mathbf{+6}$

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons are there in a $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ ion? (Cr is $Z = 24$.)
questions.solution:
Chromium is $[\text{Ar}]3d^{5}4s^{1}$. Forming $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ removes the $4s$ electron and two $3d$ electrons, leaving $[\text{Ar}]3d^{3}$.

By Hund's rule those three occupy separate orbitals with parallel spins, so there are $\mathbf{3}$ unpaired electrons.

The magnetic moment is then $\sqrt{3 \times 5} = 3.87\ \text{BM}$.

questions.q: How many moles of $\mathrm{I_2}$ are liberated when 1 mole of potassium dichromate react with potassium iodide ?
questions.solution:
$\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + 6\mathrm{I^-} + 14\mathrm{H^+} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + 3\mathrm{I_2} + 7\mathrm{H_2O}$

Each Cr gains 3 electrons, so one dichromate takes 6 electrons, enough to oxidise 6 iodide ions to **3** moles of $\mathrm{I_2}$.

questions.q: Explain the lanthanoid contraction and its causes. Discuss three of its consequences, including its effect on the second and third transition series, and explain why lanthanoids are difficult to separate from one another.
questions.solution:
**What it is.** The **lanthanoid contraction** is the steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanoid series from cerium to lutetium.

$\text{La}^{3+}$: $106\ \text{pm}$ down to $\text{Lu}^{3+}$: $85\ \text{pm}$ — a fall of about $21\ \text{pm}$ across fourteen elements, so roughly $1.5\ \text{pm}$ per element. Small per step, substantial in total.

**The cause.** Across the series, each added electron enters the **$4f$** subshell.

The $4f$ orbitals have a **diffuse, deeply buried shape** and **shield the outer electrons very poorly** from the nucleus. The shielding order runs $s > p > d > f$, so $f$ electrons are the worst shielders of all.

So with each element the **nuclear charge increases by one** while the **shielding barely improves**. The **effective nuclear charge felt by the outer electrons therefore rises steadily**, pulling the whole electron cloud inward.

The contraction is gradual because the effect is a small imbalance repeated fourteen times, not a sudden change.

**Consequence 1: the second and third transition series have nearly identical radii.**

This is the most important consequence, and it reaches well outside the lanthanoids themselves.

Normally radii increase down a group as a new shell is added. Between the **second (4d)** and **third (5d)** transition series, however, the fourteen lanthanoids intervene — and their contraction almost exactly **cancels** the expected increase.

Zr $160\ \text{pm}$ / Hf $159\ \text{pm}$

Nb $143$ / Ta $143$

Mo $136$ / W $137$

The pairs are effectively the same size, and since chemical behaviour depends heavily on size and charge, they have **almost identical chemistry**. Zirconium and hafnium are notoriously among the hardest pairs of elements to separate — which matters commercially, because hafnium absorbs neutrons strongly and zirconium does not, so nuclear-grade zirconium must be hafnium-free.

The third series is also unusually **dense** for the same reason: nearly the same volume, roughly twice the mass. Osmium and iridium are the densest elements known.

**Consequence 2: basicity of the hydroxides decreases across the series.**

As the ionic radius falls, the charge density of $\text{M}^{3+}$ rises, so the metal holds the hydroxide oxygen more tightly and releases $\text{OH}^{-}$ less readily.

$\text{La(OH)}_3$ is the most basic and $\text{Lu(OH)}_3$ the least.

This graded difference is exploited in **fractional precipitation**, one of the classical separation methods.

**Consequence 3: a small but usable gradation in solubility and complex stability.**

Complex stability **increases** slightly across the series as the ions get smaller and more polarising, and salt solubilities change gradually in step. These differences are the basis of **ion-exchange chromatography**, the modern separation method.

**Why lanthanoids are so hard to separate.**

Three reasons compound each other.

**They almost all show the same oxidation state, $+3$.** Because the $4f$ electrons are buried and well shielded, they take little part in bonding. So the series offers none of the chemical variety that makes transition metals easy to separate by oxidation and reduction. Cerium ($+4$) and europium ($+2$) are the exceptions, and are consequently the **easiest two to separate** — which itself demonstrates that the shared oxidation state is the real obstacle.

**Their sizes differ by only about $1.5\ \text{pm}$ per element.** Since chemistry is governed by charge and size, and the charge is identical while the sizes are nearly so, **adjacent lanthanoids behave almost identically**.

**The $4f$ electrons are shielded from the ligand field.** Being buried beneath the $5s$ and $5p$ shells, they barely feel their surroundings — so the ligand-field effects that distinguish transition metal complexes so sharply are largely absent here.

**How separation is actually done.** The classical methods — fractional crystallisation and fractional precipitation — required **hundreds or thousands** of repetitions to exploit the tiny differences, which is why pure lanthanoids were rare and expensive for so long.

Modern practice uses **ion-exchange chromatography** and **solvent extraction**, which repeat that small difference automatically over many theoretical plates. It is the same tiny gradation being used, simply amplified mechanically rather than by hand.
